newsitem.title: EGYPT: Hostile spotlight shines on Egyptian Shi'ites.
newsitem.headline: Hostile spotlight shines on Egyptian Shi'ites.

text.p: A hostile spotlight shone this week on Egypt's Shi'ite community, a tiny and obscure minority in a sea of more than 50 million staunch Sunni Moslems.
Government statements, reflecting the views of ordinary Egyptians for whom the Shi'ites are a distant and heretical sect, gave the impression their very faith might be illegal.
The Interior Ministry set the tone on Monday with the announcement it had caught 56 members of a secret Egyptian Shi'ite group trying to spread Iranian and Shi'ite concepts.

"It planned to flood the country with publications and cassette tapes designed to propagate Shi'ite thought, distort the constants of orthodox religion, divide the Islamic nation and promote certain deviant ideas," the ministry said.

The cabinet discussed the Shi'ite menace on Wednesday, probably for the first time in living memory, and decided to set up a committee. "It will consider the legislation which counters the expansion of these ideas, which are injurious to the values of Islam," said government spokesman Safwat el-Sherif.

The Egyptian government has often accused the government of Shi'ite Moslem Iran of financing and supporting the Islamist militants fighting the police in the south of Egypt. More than 1,000 people have been killed in the conflict since 1992.
Historian Gamal Badawi, who is also editor of the opposition party newspaper al-Wafd, took up the cudgels against Shi'ites on Thursday in a vitriolic attack on their role in Egypt's history.

The Fatimids, Shi'ite invaders from North Africa, built the city of Cairo in the 10th century and ruled the country for 200 years until Saladin of Crusader fame abolished their caliphate in 1171 AD. Egypt has been solidly Sunni ever since.

The Shi'ites differ with the Sunnis originally over who should have led the Moslem community on the death of the Prophet Mohammad. Many differences over doctrine, religious law and political organisation have since developed.
For hundreds of years Iran has been the bastion of Shi'ite Islam and the Iranian revolution in 1979 made Sunni rulers in the Arab world especially wary of Shi'ite missionaries.
Badawi said Shi'ites had long sought to regain a foothold in Egypt but until recently moderate and sensible Egyptians had always resisted their esoteric doctrines.

He cited the case of the Bohara, a Shi'ite sect from India, who flocked to Egypt in the 1980s under the patronage of the late president Anwar Sadat and spent millions on restoring mosques associated with Fatimid rule.

"Unfortunately, there has been a Shi'ite penetration of Egypt without the government noticing. They now have a strong presence among intellectuals and youngsters," Badawi said in a front-page editorial in his newspaper.
"Some writers, including myself, have shouted ourselves hoarse warning of the Shi'ite danger heading for Egypt but nobody has done anything," he added.

But Egyptians who follow religious trends said Shi'ites remained a tiny minority, many of them immigrants from Shi'ite Moslem communities in other Arab countries, even if some young Islamists admire features of Shi'ite doctrine.
"I don't think all this hullaballoo is justified. The number of Shi'ites is tiny and there's no way you can say Shi'ism is illegal," said one expert, who asked not to be named.
A government spokesman also tried to play down the affair, denying there was any plan to outlaw Shi'ism.
"The trouble with the group of 56 was their contacts with external elements, meaning Iran, and I believe with Hizbollah (the Shi'ite organisation in Lebanon)," he said.
"The Shi'ites in Egypt are an extremely marginal minority," added the spokesman. He could not say how many there are but it is believed to be only a few hundred.
Officials at the Iranian interests section, a natural focus for Shi'ite affairs, were not available on Thursday.
